--- title: DATASCI 350 - Data Science Computing subtitle: Lecture 22 - SQL Revision with DuckDB lang: en-GB author: - name: Danilo Freire email: danilo.freire@emory.edu affiliations: "Department of Data and Decision Sciences
Emory University" format: clean-revealjs: self-contained: false code-overflow: wrap footer: "[SQL with DuckDB](https://danilofreire.github.io/datasci350/lectures/lecture-22/22-sql-revision.html)" transition: slide transition-speed: default scrollable: true engine: python3 execute: freeze: auto cache: true revealjs-plugins: - fontawesome - multimodal editor: render-on-save: true --- # Hello again! 😊 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} # Brief recap 📚 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Parallel computing fundamentals ### Where lecture 21 left us :::{style="margin-top: 30px; font-size: 23px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Last class: [parallel and scalable computing]{.alert} - `map`, `joblib` and `concurrent.futures` - [Big O]{.alert}: parallelism divides the time, but not the growth rate - [Amdahl's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law): the serial share limits the speed-up - [The GIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_interpreter_lock): threads for waiting, processes for computing - [Dask]{.alert}: lazy arrays and DataFrames for data bigger than RAM ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - Some engines [use all your cores]{.alert} with no setup - DuckDB is one of them, and today we use it to revise [SQL]{.alert} - All queries run on the [WDI panel]{.alert} from Lecture 19 - [Download it here](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/raw/refs/heads/main/lectures/lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet) or use the path `../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet` :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -10px;"} [![](figures/parallel.png){width="52%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/parallel.png"} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Lecture overview ### What we will cover today :::{style="margin-top: 12px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} ::::{.column width="50%"} [1. Why SQL and why DuckDB]{.alert} - A declarative language every engine speaks - `import duckdb` is the whole setup [2. First queries]{.alert} - `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT` - `IN`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE`, and the order a query runs in [3. Aggregating]{.alert} - `COUNT`, `AVG`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING` - What `COUNT` does when values are missing :::: ::::{.column width="50%"} [4. NULLs, CASE and windows]{.alert} - `IS NULL`, `COALESCE`, income bands with `CASE` - Window functions: a group mean and a rank on every row [5. Joins]{.alert} - Primary keys, foreign keys, and the `ON` clause - `INNER`, `LEFT`, `FULL OUTER` on two tiny tables [6. DuckDB and pandas]{.alert} - Querying a `pandas` DataFrame by its variable name - Handing a result back with `.df()` - DuckDB on 200 million rows :::: ::: ::: # Why SQL, why DuckDB 🦆 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Why SQL ### You describe the answer, the engine finds it :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="52%"} - [SQL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL) is a language for [asking questions of tables]{.alert} - It is [relational]{.alert}: tables of rows and columns, combined with joins - It is [declarative]{.alert}: you say what you want, and the engine decides how - No loops, no variables, no input/output code - The engine can reorder the query, skip columns, or use every core - SQL is [about fifty years old](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SQL), and tech job adverts list it [about as often as Python](https://finance.yahoo.com/sectors/technology/articles/research-sql-rivals-python-america-131700698.html) - `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` work the same in DuckDB, SQLite, PostgreSQL, BigQuery and Snowflake ::: :::{.column width="48%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -10px;"} [![](figures/duckdb-docs-sql-2026.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/duckdb-docs-sql-2026.png"} :::{style="font-size: 17px;"} DuckDB's SQL introduction: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Why DuckDB for a revision class ### An in-process engine with no setup :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="52%"} - [Zero setup]{.alert}: `pip install duckdb`, then `import duckdb` - Unlike [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/admin.html), there is no server, user or password - [In-process]{.alert}: it runs inside your Python session, [like SQLite](https://www.sqlite.org/) - [Reads files by name]{.alert}: a Parquet or CSV path goes straight in `FROM` - It reads a pandas DataFrame by its variable name too - [Columnar]{.alert} and [parallel]{.alert}, so the same `GROUP BY` works on 200 million rows - Version used here: [DuckDB 1.5.5](https://duckdb.org/2026/03/09/announcing-duckdb-150) ::: :::{.column width="48%"} :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: -10px;"} [![](figures/duckdb-home-2026.png){width="100%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/duckdb-home-2026.png"} :::{style="font-size: 17px;"} Source: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: # First queries {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## What a table is ### Rows, columns and one value per cell :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - A [table]{.alert} is a grid: each [row]{.alert} is an observation, each [column]{.alert} a variable - Each column has one [type]{.alert}. Ours are text (`VARCHAR`), whole numbers (`SMALLINT`) and decimals (`DOUBLE`) - Other common types: `BOOLEAN` (true or false), `DATE` and `TIMESTAMP` - A cell holds one value, or nothing: `NULL` - The [WDI panel]{.alert}: 217 countries, 8 indicators, 34 years (1990 to 2023) - The number is always in `value`. The `indicator` column says what it measures - So most queries start with `WHERE indicator = '...'`, or they mix dollars with years of life - In pandas terms: a table is a DataFrame, a column is a Series, and there is no index ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="text-align: center; font-size: 23px;"} Six rows of the panel, for Brazil in 2019 and 2020: | country | iso3 | indicator | year | value | |---|---|---|---|---| | Brazil | BRA | gdp_per_capita | 2019 | 8771.44 | | Brazil | BRA | gdp_per_capita | 2020 | 8435.01 | | Brazil | BRA | internet_users_pct | 2019 | 73.91 | | Brazil | BRA | internet_users_pct | 2020 | 81.34 | | Brazil | BRA | life_expectancy | 2019 | 75.81 | | Brazil | BRA | life_expectancy | 2020 | 74.51 | ::: :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 12px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 19px; margin-top: 15px;"} No two rows share the same `country`, `indicator` and `year`. Together they identify a row: the idea behind a [primary key]{.alert} ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Querying a Parquet file ### The file path goes in the FROM clause :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - The WDI panel is a Parquet file with 59,024 rows - [Download it here](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/raw/refs/heads/main/lectures/lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet) or use the path `../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet` - `duckdb.sql()` takes a query string and returns a result you can print - The path goes in [single quotes]{.alert}: single quotes mean text, double quotes a column name - No `read_parquet`, connection or `fetchall()` needed. DuckDB handles it - The [column types]{.alert} under the names come from the file ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 24px;"} ::: {#684bdbc9 .cell cache='true' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import duckdb duckdb.sql(""" SELECT * FROM '../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet' LIMIT 5 """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ┌─────────┬─────────┬────────────────┬───────┬──────────────────┐ │ country │ iso3 │ indicator │ year │ value │ │ varchar │ varchar │ varchar │ int16 │ double │ ├─────────┼─────────┼────────────────┼───────┼──────────────────┤ │ Aruba │ ABW │ co2_per_capita │ 1990 │ 3.20303411789078 │ │ Aruba │ ABW │ co2_per_capita │ 1991 │ 3.43571688721622 │ │ Aruba │ ABW │ co2_per_capita │ 1992 │ 3.6345192377364 │ │ Aruba │ ABW │ co2_per_capita │ 1993 │ 3.41453484426953 │ │ Aruba │ ABW │ co2_per_capita │ 1994 │ 3.68322701204975 │ └─────────┴─────────┴────────────────┴───────┴──────────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Creating a view ### One name for the file :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="44%"} - A [view]{.alert} is a saved query that behaves like a table - `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW wdi AS ...` names the query `wdi` - Later queries say `FROM wdi`, with no file path - A view holds no data: DuckDB re-reads the file each time - `OR REPLACE` overwrites an old view, so the cell is safe to re-run - [`COUNT(DISTINCT country)`]{.alert} counts the different values in a column - The view disappears when Python restarts ::: :::{.column width="56%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#9404b1a2 .cell cache='true' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW wdi AS SELECT * FROM '../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet' """) duckdb.sql(""" SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT country) AS countries, COUNT(DISTINCT indicator) AS indicators FROM wdi """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ┌────────┬───────────┬────────────┐ │ n_rows │ countries │ indicators │ │ int64 │ int64 │ int64 │ ├────────┼───────────┼────────────┤ │ 59024 │ 217 │ 8 │ └────────┴───────────┴────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## DESCRIBE and SUMMARIZE ### Two commands to run before any query :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="44%"} - Run both before writing a query, to learn the column names - [`DESCRIBE`]{.alert} lists the columns and their types - `country`, `iso3` and `indicator` are text (`VARCHAR`), so filters on them need single quotes - [`SUMMARIZE`]{.alert} adds min, max, count and the share of missing values - 11.06% of `value` is missing. `country` and `year` have no gaps - Its result is a table, so we can `SELECT` from it - In pandas: `df.dtypes` and `df.describe()` ::: :::{.column width="56%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#aaa59798 .cell cache='true' execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql("DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM wdi") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ┌─────────────┬─────────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┬─────────┐ │ column_name │ column_type │ null │ key │ default │ extra │ │ varchar │ varchar │ varchar │ varchar │ varchar │ varchar │ ├─────────────┼─────────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┼─────────┤ │ country │ VARCHAR │ YES │ NULL │ NULL │ NULL │ │ iso3 │ VARCHAR │ YES │ NULL │ NULL │ NULL │ │ indicator │ VARCHAR │ YES │ NULL │ NULL │ NULL │ │ year │ SMALLINT │ YES │ NULL │ NULL │ NULL │ │ value │ DOUBLE │ YES │ NULL │ NULL │ NULL │ └─────────────┴─────────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: {#070e2190 .cell cache='true' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT column_name, min, max, null_percentage FROM (SUMMARIZE SELECT country, year, value FROM wdi) """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ┌─────────────┬─────────────┬──────────────┬─────────────────┐ │ column_name │ min │ max │ null_percentage │ │ varchar │ varchar │ varchar │ decimal(9,2) │ ├─────────────┼─────────────┼──────────────┼─────────────────┤ │ country │ Afghanistan │ Zimbabwe │ 0.00 │ │ year │ 1990 │ 2023 │ 0.00 │ │ value │ 0.0 │ 1438069596.0 │ 11.06 │ └─────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┴─────────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## SELECT, aliases, ORDER BY, LIMIT ### Picking columns and sorting the result :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="48%"} - The query is a Python string passed to `duckdb.sql()` - Keywords are upper case by convention, but `select` works too, and `Country` finds `country` - `SELECT` lists the columns you want. `*` means all of them - It can compute new columns, like `ROUND(value, 0)` - [`AS`]{.alert} gives a column a new name, called an [alias]{.alert} - [`ORDER BY value DESC`]{.alert} sorts high to low. `ASC`, low to high, is the default - [`LIMIT`]{.alert} keeps the first rows, like `.head()` in pandas ::: :::{.column width="52%"} :::{style="font-size: 24px;"} ::: {#5ae48150 .cell cache='true' execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, year, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_pc FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND year = 2020 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 5 """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` ┌─────────────┬───────┬──────────┐ │ country │ year │ gdp_pc │ │ varchar │ int16 │ double │ ├─────────────┼───────┼──────────┤ │ Monaco │ 2020 │ 161263.0 │ │ Luxembourg │ 2020 │ 105274.0 │ │ Bermuda │ 2020 │ 98846.0 │ │ Isle of Man │ 2020 │ 86595.0 │ │ Switzerland │ 2020 │ 86294.0 │ └─────────────┴───────┴──────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## WHERE with AND, OR and NOT ### Filtering rows with WHERE :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="48%"} - [`WHERE`]{.alert} keeps rows where the condition is true, like boolean indexing in pandas - Comparisons: `=`, `<>` (not equal), `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` - [`AND`]{.alert} needs both sides true. [`OR`]{.alert} needs either - [`NOT`]{.alert} flips a condition: `NOT country = 'Japan'` would keep only Brazil - Text goes in single quotes, and the match is case-sensitive - The brackets matter, because `AND` is applied before `OR` - Four rows: Brazil on 6,818 and 8,435, Japan on 31,779 and 35,363 ::: :::{.column width="52%"} :::{style="font-size: 24px;"} ::: {#b1e87090 .cell cache='true' execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, year, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_pc FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND (year = 2000 OR year = 2020) AND (country = 'Brazil' OR country = 'Japan') ORDER BY country, year """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` ┌─────────┬───────┬─────────┐ │ country │ year │ gdp_pc │ │ varchar │ int16 │ double │ ├─────────┼───────┼─────────┤ │ Brazil │ 2000 │ 6818.0 │ │ Brazil │ 2020 │ 8435.0 │ │ Japan │ 2000 │ 31779.0 │ │ Japan │ 2020 │ 35363.0 │ └─────────┴───────┴─────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{style="background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 12px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 18px; margin-top: 10px;"} Without the brackets, the query returns 496 rows: GDP for every country in 2000, all of Brazil's 2020 rows, and every Japanese row ::: ::: ::: ::: ## IN and BETWEEN ### Shorter ways to write the same conditions :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="46%"} - [`IN`]{.alert} replaces a chain of `OR`s on one column - `country IN ('Brazil', 'China')` means `country = 'Brazil' OR country = 'China'` - [`BETWEEN`]{.alert} includes both ends: 2018 to 2020 covers three years - The low end goes first. `BETWEEN 2020 AND 2018` returns nothing - In pandas: `.isin([...])` and `.between(2018, 2020)` - Six countries × three years = 18 rows. `LIMIT 6` shows Brazil and China ::: :::{.column width="54%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#46644837 .cell cache='true' execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, year, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_pc FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND country IN ('Brazil', 'China', 'Germany', 'India', 'Japan', 'United States') AND year BETWEEN 2018 AND 2020 ORDER BY country, year LIMIT 6 """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` ┌─────────┬───────┬─────────┐ │ country │ year │ gdp_pc │ │ varchar │ int16 │ double │ ├─────────┼───────┼─────────┤ │ Brazil │ 2018 │ 8722.0 │ │ Brazil │ 2019 │ 8771.0 │ │ Brazil │ 2020 │ 8435.0 │ │ China │ 2018 │ 9799.0 │ │ China │ 2019 │ 10356.0 │ │ China │ 2020 │ 10573.0 │ └─────────┴───────┴─────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## LIKE and ILIKE ### Matching part of a text value :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="44%"} - [`LIKE`]{.alert} matches part of a text value - `%` means any characters, or none. `_` means exactly one character - `'United%'` starts with United, `'%States'` ends with States, `'%King%'` contains King - [`DISTINCT`]{.alert} removes duplicates. Without it, each country appears once per indicator and year - `LIKE` is case-sensitive, so `'united%'` finds nothing - [`ILIKE`]{.alert} ignores case, and finds the same three countries - In pandas: `.str.startswith()` or `.str.contains()` ::: :::{.column width="56%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#208fa33c .cell cache='true' execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT DISTINCT country FROM wdi WHERE country LIKE 'United%' ORDER BY country """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` ┌──────────────────────┐ │ country │ │ varchar │ ├──────────────────────┤ │ United Arab Emirates │ │ United Kingdom │ │ United States │ └──────────────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: {#3fb20da3 .cell cache='true' execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT DISTINCT country FROM wdi WHERE country ILIKE 'united%' ORDER BY country """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` ┌──────────────────────┐ │ country │ │ varchar │ ├──────────────────────┤ │ United Arab Emirates │ │ United Kingdom │ │ United States │ └──────────────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## One query, one clause at a time ### Every clause you have met, in one query :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="45%"} :::{style="text-align: center; font-size: 22px; margin-top: 10px; margin-bottom: 30px;"} | Clause | What it does | |---|---| | `FROM wdi` | picks the table | | `WHERE` | keeps 6 of 59,024 rows | | `SELECT` | picks 3 columns, rounds one | | `ORDER BY` | sorts by value | | `LIMIT` | keeps 3 rows | ::: - You have met every clause here - Read a query from `FROM`, because that is where the engine starts - Three rows survive: the United States (59,534), Germany (42,373) and Japan (35,363) - We build on this query for the rest of the lecture ::: :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#44b270dd .cell cache='true' execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, year, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_pc FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND country IN ('Brazil', 'China', 'Germany', 'India', 'Japan', 'United States') AND year = 2020 ORDER BY value DESC LIMIT 3 """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` ┌───────────────┬───────┬─────────┐ │ country │ year │ gdp_pc │ │ varchar │ int16 │ double │ ├───────────────┼───────┼─────────┤ │ United States │ 2020 │ 59534.0 │ │ Germany │ 2020 │ 42373.0 │ │ Japan │ 2020 │ 35363.0 │ └───────────────┴───────┴─────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## The order a query really runs in ### How the engine evaluates a query :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{style="text-align: center;"} [![](figures/sql-evaluation-order.png){width="60%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/sql-evaluation-order.png"} ::: :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - You write `SELECT` first, but the engine runs it fifth - `FROM` finds the rows, `WHERE` filters them, `GROUP BY` makes groups, `HAVING` filters groups, then `SELECT` builds the output - `ORDER BY` sorts what `SELECT` produced, and `LIMIT` runs last of all ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - An aggregate cannot go in `WHERE`: the groups do not exist yet - Standard SQL rejects a `SELECT` alias in `WHERE`, because the alias does not exist yet. DuckDB allows it - pandas writes the steps in this order: `df[mask].groupby(...).agg(...)` ::: ::: ::: # Aggregating {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## GROUP BY {#sec-group-by} ### One row of output per group :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="48%"} - An [aggregate function]{.alert} turns many rows into one number - The common ones: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG` (mean), `MIN`, `MAX` - Without `GROUP BY`, the whole table is one group, so you get one row - [`GROUP BY country`]{.alert} makes six groups, so six rows - Every column in `SELECT` must be in `GROUP BY` or inside an aggregate - `SELECT country, value ... GROUP BY country` fails: each group has 14 values, and SQL will not pick one - `n` is 14: the years 2010 to 2023. In pandas: `.groupby("country").agg(...)` - Two grouping columns give one row per pair: [[Appendix 04]{.button}](#sec-appendix-04) ::: :::{.column width="52%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#dca829a4 .cell cache='true' execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, COUNT(value) AS n, ROUND(AVG(value), 0) AS mean_gdp FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND country IN ('Brazil', 'China', 'Germany', 'India', 'Japan', 'United States') AND year >= 2010 GROUP BY country ORDER BY mean_gdp DESC """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` ┌───────────────┬───────┬──────────┐ │ country │ n │ mean_gdp │ │ varchar │ int64 │ double │ ├───────────────┼───────┼──────────┤ │ United States │ 14 │ 58330.0 │ │ Germany │ 14 │ 42448.0 │ │ Japan │ 14 │ 35682.0 │ │ China │ 14 │ 9017.0 │ │ Brazil │ 14 │ 8923.0 │ │ India │ 14 │ 1694.0 │ └───────────────┴───────┴──────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## WHERE and HAVING ### Filtering before and after grouping :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="48%"} - `WHERE` filters rows [before]{.alert} grouping. [`HAVING`]{.alert} filters groups [after]{.alert} - Only `HAVING` can use an aggregate, because the groups exist by then - "Which years count?" is about rows, so it goes in `WHERE` - "Which countries qualify?" is about groups, so it goes in `HAVING` - `HAVING AVG(value) > 30000` keeps three countries - China (9,017), Brazil (8,923) and India (1,694) drop out - `ORDER BY` can use the alias `mean_gdp`, because it runs after `SELECT` ::: :::{.column width="52%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#d293314e .cell cache='true' execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, COUNT(value) AS n, ROUND(AVG(value), 0) AS mean_gdp FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND country IN ('Brazil', 'China', 'Germany', 'India', 'Japan', 'United States') AND year >= 2010 GROUP BY country HAVING AVG(value) > 30000 ORDER BY mean_gdp DESC """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` ┌───────────────┬───────┬──────────┐ │ country │ n │ mean_gdp │ │ varchar │ int64 │ double │ ├───────────────┼───────┼──────────┤ │ United States │ 14 │ 58330.0 │ │ Germany │ 14 │ 42448.0 │ │ Japan │ 14 │ 35682.0 │ └───────────────┴───────┴──────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## COUNT(\*) and COUNT(value) ### Counting rows and counting values :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="48%"} - [`COUNT(*)`]{.alert} counts rows - [`COUNT(value)`]{.alert} counts only the rows where `value` is present - The difference is the number of missing values - `AVG`, `SUM`, `MIN` and `MAX` skip missing values without warning - 217 countries a year: 25 missing in 1990, 18 in 2000, 9 in 2020 - So GDP coverage [improves]{.alert} over time - In pandas: `len(df)` against `df["value"].count()` - Check this before you trust a mean ::: :::{.column width="52%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#91f18e1a .cell cache='true' execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT year, COUNT(*) AS n_rows, COUNT(value) AS with_value, COUNT(*) - COUNT(value) AS missing FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND year IN (1990, 2000, 2020) GROUP BY year ORDER BY year """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` ┌───────┬────────┬────────────┬─────────┐ │ year │ n_rows │ with_value │ missing │ │ int16 │ int64 │ int64 │ int64 │ ├───────┼────────┼────────────┼─────────┤ │ 1990 │ 217 │ 192 │ 25 │ │ 2000 │ 217 │ 199 │ 18 │ │ 2020 │ 217 │ 208 │ 9 │ └───────┴────────┴────────────┴─────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: # NULLs, CASE and windows {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Missing values ### Working with NULL :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="48%"} - [NULL]{.alert} means "unknown". It is not zero, and not an empty string - Any comparison with NULL gives NULL, so `NULL = NULL` never matches - Test with [`IS NULL`]{.alert} or [`IS NOT NULL`]{.alert} - [`COALESCE(a, b)`]{.alert} returns `a`, or `b` if `a` is NULL - Yemen has no 2020 GDP figure, so it shows 0 here - Filling with 0 is a choice. A mean over this column would be wrong - `COALESCE` fills a missing value. A missing [row]{.alert} needs a `LEFT JOIN` - In pandas, NULL is `NaN`, and `.fillna(0)` does this ::: :::{.column width="52%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#4b4f0aa3 .cell cache='true' execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, ROUND(COALESCE(value, 0), 0) AS gdp_filled FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND year = 2020 AND country IN ('Brazil', 'China', 'Germany', 'India', 'Japan', 'United States', 'Yemen, Rep.') ORDER BY country """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` ┌───────────────┬────────────┐ │ country │ gdp_filled │ │ varchar │ double │ ├───────────────┼────────────┤ │ Brazil │ 8435.0 │ │ China │ 10573.0 │ │ Germany │ 42373.0 │ │ India │ 1807.0 │ │ Japan │ 35363.0 │ │ United States │ 59534.0 │ │ Yemen, Rep. │ 0.0 │ └───────────────┴────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## CASE ### Writing an if-else ladder inside a SELECT :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="45%"} - [`CASE`]{.alert} is an if-else ladder inside `SELECT` - `WHEN` gives a condition, and `THEN` the value to use if it holds - Tests run top to bottom, and the first true one wins - `ELSE` catches the rest, and `END` closes the ladder. Without `ELSE`, unmatched rows get NULL - The cut-offs are the World Bank's FY24 income bands. The Bank applies them to GNI per capita, so here they are a rough guide - `IS NULL` comes first on purpose. Lower down, Yemen would fall to `ELSE` as "Low income" - The result is a new column you can group, join, or export ::: :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#d7ca228f .cell cache='true' execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_pc, CASE WHEN value IS NULL THEN 'No data' WHEN value >= 13846 THEN 'High income' WHEN value >= 4466 THEN 'Upper middle' WHEN value >= 1136 THEN 'Lower middle' ELSE 'Low income' END AS income_band FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND year = 2020 AND country IN ('Brazil', 'China', 'Germany', 'India', 'Japan', 'United States', 'Yemen, Rep.') ORDER BY value DESC NULLS LAST """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` ┌───────────────┬─────────┬──────────────┐ │ country │ gdp_pc │ income_band │ │ varchar │ double │ varchar │ ├───────────────┼─────────┼──────────────┤ │ United States │ 59534.0 │ High income │ │ Germany │ 42373.0 │ High income │ │ Japan │ 35363.0 │ High income │ │ China │ 10573.0 │ Upper middle │ │ Brazil │ 8435.0 │ Upper middle │ │ India │ 1807.0 │ Lower middle │ │ Yemen, Rep. │ NULL │ No data │ └───────────────┴─────────┴──────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Window functions {#sec-windows} ### A group-level number on every row :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="45%"} - `GROUP BY year` would collapse these 12 rows into 2 - A [window function]{.alert} keeps every row and adds a group number beside it - [`OVER`]{.alert} turns an aggregate into a window function - [`PARTITION BY year`]{.alert} makes one [window]{.alert}, a set of rows, per year. No rows are lost - `year_mean` repeats on each row of its year: 20,885 in 2000, 26,347 in 2020 - In pandas: `.groupby("year")["value"].transform("mean")` ::: :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#b71d01ec .cell cache='true' execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, year, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_pc, ROUND(AVG(value) OVER (PARTITION BY year), 0) AS year_mean FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND country IN ('Brazil', 'China', 'Germany', 'India', 'Japan', 'United States') AND year IN (2000, 2020) ORDER BY year, value DESC """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` ┌───────────────┬───────┬─────────┬───────────┐ │ country │ year │ gdp_pc │ year_mean │ │ varchar │ int16 │ double │ double │ ├───────────────┼───────┼─────────┼───────────┤ │ United States │ 2000 │ 48616.0 │ 20885.0 │ │ Germany │ 2000 │ 35104.0 │ 20885.0 │ │ Japan │ 2000 │ 31779.0 │ 20885.0 │ │ Brazil │ 2000 │ 6818.0 │ 20885.0 │ │ China │ 2000 │ 2237.0 │ 20885.0 │ │ India │ 2000 │ 757.0 │ 20885.0 │ │ United States │ 2020 │ 59534.0 │ 26347.0 │ │ Germany │ 2020 │ 42373.0 │ 26347.0 │ │ Japan │ 2020 │ 35363.0 │ 26347.0 │ │ China │ 2020 │ 10573.0 │ 26347.0 │ │ Brazil │ 2020 │ 8435.0 │ 26347.0 │ │ India │ 2020 │ 1807.0 │ 26347.0 │ └───────────────┴───────┴─────────┴───────────┘ 12 rows 4 columns ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Ranking with a window ### RANK() needs an ORDER BY inside OVER :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="45%"} - [`RANK()`]{.alert} numbers rows by the `ORDER BY` inside `OVER` - The inner `ORDER BY` sets the ranks. The outer one sorts the printed table - No `PARTITION BY`: one window for the whole result - Ties share a rank, and the next is skipped: 1, 2, 2, 4 - `DENSE_RANK()` gives 1, 2, 2, 3, and `ROW_NUMBER()` never ties - The United States ranks 1 (59,534), and India 6 (1,807) - `WHERE` runs first, so only these six countries are ranked - Add `PARTITION BY year` to rank within each year ::: :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#fad31567 .cell cache='true' execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_pc, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY value DESC) AS rank_2020 FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND country IN ('Brazil', 'China', 'Germany', 'India', 'Japan', 'United States') AND year = 2020 ORDER BY rank_2020 """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` ┌───────────────┬─────────┬───────────┐ │ country │ gdp_pc │ rank_2020 │ │ varchar │ double │ int64 │ ├───────────────┼─────────┼───────────┤ │ United States │ 59534.0 │ 1 │ │ Germany │ 42373.0 │ 2 │ │ Japan │ 35363.0 │ 3 │ │ China │ 10573.0 │ 4 │ │ Brazil │ 8435.0 │ 5 │ │ India │ 1807.0 │ 6 │ └───────────────┴─────────┴───────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: # Joins {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Two small tables ### Keys, and the two tables we will join :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="42%"} - A [table]{.alert} stores its data, unlike the `wdi` view - `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` builds `gdp2020` from a query - `CREATE TABLE (col TYPE, ...)` declares empty columns. `INSERT INTO ... VALUES` adds rows - A [primary key]{.alert} identifies each row, with no duplicates or NULLs: `iso3` in `regions` - A [foreign key]{.alert} points at another table's primary key. `iso3` in `gdp2020` plays that role, but we never declare it, so `JPN` can sit there with no partner - Six rows in `gdp2020`, seven in `regions` - Mismatches: [`JPN`]{.alert} has GDP but no region. [`KOR`]{.alert} and [`AUS`]{.alert} have a region but no GDP - East Asia holds two codes, which matters in the exercise ::: :::{.column width="58%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#bd374ae0 .cell cache='true' execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gdp2020 AS SELECT country, iso3, ROUND(value, 0) AS gdp_per_capita FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'gdp_per_capita' AND year = 2020 AND iso3 IN ('USA','BRA','CHN','IND','DEU','JPN') """) duckdb.sql(""" CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE regions (iso3 VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, region VARCHAR) """) duckdb.sql(""" INSERT INTO regions VALUES ('USA', 'North America'), ('BRA', 'Latin America'), ('CHN', 'East Asia'), ('IND', 'South Asia'), ('DEU', 'Europe'), ('KOR', 'East Asia'), ('AUS', 'Oceania') """) duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM regions ORDER BY iso3") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` ┌─────────┬───────────────┐ │ iso3 │ region │ │ varchar │ varchar │ ├─────────┼───────────────┤ │ AUS │ Oceania │ │ BRA │ Latin America │ │ CHN │ East Asia │ │ DEU │ Europe │ │ IND │ South Asia │ │ KOR │ East Asia │ │ USA │ North America │ └─────────┴───────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Reading a join ### The ON clause and table aliases :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="46%"} - A [`JOIN`]{.alert} combines two tables into one wider result - [`ON`]{.alert} says which columns must match: `iso3` on both sides - Each matching pair of rows becomes one output row - `AS g` and `AS r` are [table aliases]{.alert}: short names for the tables - `g.country` means "`country` from `gdp2020`". Prefix every column this way - The join type goes before `JOIN`. `INNER` is the default - In pandas: `pd.merge(gdp2020, regions, on="iso3")` - The next three slides run this with three join types ::: :::{.column width="54%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ```sql SELECT g.country, r.region, g.gdp_per_capita FROM gdp2020 AS g INNER JOIN regions AS r ON g.iso3 = r.iso3 ORDER BY g.country ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## INNER JOIN ### Only the rows that match on both sides :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="46%"} - An [`INNER JOIN`]{.alert} keeps only the codes in both tables - Six rows on the left, seven on the right, [five]{.alert} out - Japan drops out: `JPN` is not in `regions` - Korea and Australia drop out too: they have no 2020 GDP row - An inner join filters silently, with no warning about lost rows - If your row count falls after a join, this is usually why - In pandas: `pd.merge(..., how="inner")` ::: :::{.column width="54%"} :::{style="font-size: 24px;"} ::: {#b342aa31 .cell cache='true' execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT g.country, r.region, g.gdp_per_capita FROM gdp2020 AS g INNER JOIN regions AS r ON g.iso3 = r.iso3 ORDER BY g.country """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ``` ┌───────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ │ country │ region │ gdp_per_capita │ │ varchar │ varchar │ double │ ├───────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┤ │ Brazil │ Latin America │ 8435.0 │ │ China │ East Asia │ 10573.0 │ │ Germany │ Europe │ 42373.0 │ │ India │ South Asia │ 1807.0 │ │ United States │ North America │ 59534.0 │ └───────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## LEFT JOIN ### Keeping every row of the left table :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 23px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="46%"} - A [`LEFT JOIN`]{.alert} keeps every row of the left table - The left table is the one in `FROM`: `gdp2020` here - [Six]{.alert} rows: Japan is back, with `NULL` for `region` - That NULL means "no partner found". Japan's 35,363 is unchanged - Korea and Australia are still missing: they exist only on the right - Swap the tables and you get a different answer, as in the exercise - The join you will use most: it adds labels without losing rows - In pandas: `pd.merge(..., how="left")` ::: :::{.column width="54%"} :::{style="font-size: 24px;"} ::: {#56353f2e .cell cache='true' execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT g.country, r.region, g.gdp_per_capita FROM gdp2020 AS g LEFT JOIN regions AS r ON g.iso3 = r.iso3 ORDER BY g.country """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` ┌───────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ │ country │ region │ gdp_per_capita │ │ varchar │ varchar │ double │ ├───────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┤ │ Brazil │ Latin America │ 8435.0 │ │ China │ East Asia │ 10573.0 │ │ Germany │ Europe │ 42373.0 │ │ India │ South Asia │ 1807.0 │ │ Japan │ NULL │ 35363.0 │ │ United States │ North America │ 59534.0 │ └───────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## FULL OUTER JOIN ### Every row from both tables survives :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 19px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="45%"} - A [`FULL OUTER JOIN`]{.alert} keeps every row from both tables, with NULLs where there is no partner - [Eight]{.alert} rows: five pairs, plus Japan, Korea and Australia - Korea and Australia have a region, but NULL `country` and `gdp_per_capita` - Japan has a country and 35,363, but NULL region columns - On these tables: 5 rows from `INNER`, 6 from `LEFT`, 8 from `FULL OUTER` - To choose a join, ask which table must survive whole, and what to do with rows that have no partner :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 10px;"} [![](figures/sql-joins.png){width="80%"}](#){data-modal-type="image" data-modal-url="figures/sql-joins.png"} :::{style="font-size: 15px;"} Our two tables and the three joins. Click to enlarge ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 23px;"} ::: {#a3bfa488 .cell cache='true' execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT g.country, r.iso3 AS region_iso3, r.region, g.gdp_per_capita FROM gdp2020 AS g FULL OUTER JOIN regions AS r ON g.iso3 = r.iso3 ORDER BY r.region NULLS LAST, r.iso3 """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` ┌───────────────┬─────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────┐ │ country │ region_iso3 │ region │ gdp_per_capita │ │ varchar │ varchar │ varchar │ double │ ├───────────────┼─────────────┼───────────────┼────────────────┤ │ China │ CHN │ East Asia │ 10573.0 │ │ NULL │ KOR │ East Asia │ NULL │ │ Germany │ DEU │ Europe │ 42373.0 │ │ Brazil │ BRA │ Latin America │ 8435.0 │ │ United States │ USA │ North America │ 59534.0 │ │ NULL │ AUS │ Oceania │ NULL │ │ India │ IND │ South Asia │ 1807.0 │ │ Japan │ NULL │ NULL │ 35363.0 │ └───────────────┴─────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Try it yourself! 🧠 {#sec-exercise-01} ### Ten minutes :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="52%"} How rich is each region, and how much data is it based on? 1. Use the `gdp2020` and `regions` tables from the joins section 2. Report one row per region 3. Count how many of that region's countries have a 2020 GDP figure 4. Compute the mean GDP per capita of that region 5. Keep every region, including the one with no GDP data at all 6. Sort by mean GDP, highest first 7. Send the region with no data to the bottom of the list ::: :::{.column width="48%"} What to look for: - Which table goes on the left if every region must survive? - East Asia has two codes but one GDP figure, so `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(g.country)` differ - Oceania has no GDP figure at all - Six regions come back :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 12px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 19px; margin-top: 12px;"} Solution: [[Appendix 01]{.button}](#sec-appendix-01) ::: ::: ::: ::: # DuckDB and pandas 🐼 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Querying a DataFrame by name ### Your Python variable becomes a SQL table :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 22px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="45%"} - DuckDB finds `df` among your Python variables and queries it by name - No registration, no copy, no conversion: it reads the DataFrame in memory - The same `SELECT` works on a file, a view or a DataFrame - `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM df` gives 59,024, like the Parquet file - You can join two DataFrames in one query ::: :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 24px;"} ::: {#91ef1ffd .cell cache='true' execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet( "../lecture-19/data/wdi_panel.parquet" ) duckdb.sql("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM df") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` ┌───────┐ │ n │ │ int64 │ ├───────┤ │ 59024 │ └───────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{style="background: rgba(230, 57, 70, 0.1); padding: 12px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 18px; margin-top: 8px;"} `country` is a pandas [category]{.alert}: a text column with a fixed list of allowed values. DuckDB calls this type an [enum]{.alert} (short for enumeration). Add `::VARCHAR` to turn it into plain text ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Handing the result back to pandas {#sec-pandas} ### Turning a result into a DataFrame :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="45%"} - [`.df()`]{.alert} turns a DuckDB result into a pandas DataFrame - `.pl()` gives a Polars DataFrame, and `.to_arrow_table()` an Arrow table - Without `.df()`, you get a DuckDB result that prints as a text table - `country::VARCHAR` turns the category back into plain text - SQL returns 18 rows, and `pivot` reshapes them into 6 rows by 3 columns - DuckDB has a `PIVOT` statement too, but reshaping reads more easily in pandas - After `.df()`, it is ordinary pandas: `.plot()`, `.to_csv()`, `seaborn`, `statsmodels` - SQL or pandas? [[Appendix 06]{.button}](#sec-appendix-06) ::: :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 21px;"} ::: {#5a301c5e .cell cache='true' execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} long = duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country::VARCHAR AS country, indicator, ROUND(value, 1) AS value FROM df WHERE year = 2020 AND iso3 IN ('USA', 'BRA', 'CHN', 'IND', 'DEU', 'JPN') AND indicator IN ('gdp_per_capita', 'life_expectancy', 'internet_users_pct') """).df() long.pivot(index="country", columns="indicator", values="value") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ```{=html}

[Dask]{.alert}: 5.39 s. [pandas]{.alert}: 9.65 s - pandas loads every column into RAM. DuckDB reads only the three columns the query uses - Why: columnar storage, vectorised execution, and all cores by default - MacBook Pro, Apple M5, 10 cores, 24 GB RAM, macOS 26.6 - Your seconds will differ, but the ranking usually holds - [Polars]{.alert} is in the same range as DuckDB (Tutorial 07) - The query and scripts: [[Appendix 07]{.button}](#sec-appendix-07) ::: ::: ::: ::: # Summary {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## What we learned today ### The vocabulary, in the order we met it :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [SQL]{.alert} is declarative: you describe the answer and the engine plans the work - [DuckDB]{.alert} needs one import and reads a Parquet file or a pandas DataFrame by name - A [view]{.alert} names a query. `DESCRIBE` and `SUMMARIZE` show what is in it - [`WHERE`]{.alert} filters rows, [`GROUP BY`]{.alert} forms groups, [`HAVING`]{.alert} filters groups. No aggregate in `WHERE` - `COUNT(*)` minus `COUNT(value)` is the number of missing values ::: :::{.column width="50%"} - A [NULL]{.alert} means unknown. `COALESCE` fills one in, and a missing row needs a join instead - [`CASE`]{.alert} builds a category column from an if-else ladder - A [window function]{.alert} keeps every row: `AVG ... OVER (PARTITION BY year)` adds the year mean, `RANK()` a position - Joins: 5 rows from `INNER`, 6 from `LEFT`, 8 from `FULL OUTER` on the same two tables - On 200 million rows, DuckDB runs the same query in [0.53 seconds]{.alert} ::: ::: ::: ## Next class {#sec-next-class} :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - [Lecture 23]{.alert}: dependency management, virtual environments and containers - Today's queries depended on your Python, your DuckDB version and your laptop - Next class we package all three into an [image]{.alert}, so anyone who runs it gets the same answer - `pip install duckdb` stops being a setup instruction and becomes a line in a `Dockerfile` ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="margin-top: -15px;"} Before then: 1. Common error messages: [[Appendix 03]{.button}](#sec-appendix-03) ::: ::: ::: ::: # Thank you very much! 😊 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} # Appendix 📚 {background-color="#1B3A6B"} ## Appendix 01: Solution to the exercise {#sec-appendix-01} :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 19px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="46%"} - `regions` goes on the left, because every region must survive - East Asia has two rows in `regions`, but `COUNT(g.country)` is 1: Korea's row has a NULL country - `COUNT(*)` would count that row and report 2 - Oceania has no GDP figure: its count is 0 and its mean is NULL - `NULLS LAST` sends Oceania to the bottom - Six regions, from North America (59,534) down to South Asia (1,807), then Oceania - Codes that appear in only one table? [[Appendix 05]{.button}](#sec-appendix-05) [[Back to the exercise]{.button}](#sec-exercise-01) ::: :::{.column width="54%"} :::{style="font-size: 20px;"} ::: {#b6fad87b .cell cache='true' execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT r.region, COUNT(g.country) AS countries_with_gdp, ROUND(AVG(g.gdp_per_capita), 0) AS mean_gdp FROM regions AS r LEFT JOIN gdp2020 AS g ON g.iso3 = r.iso3 GROUP BY r.region ORDER BY mean_gdp DESC NULLS LAST """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ``` ┌───────────────┬────────────────────┬──────────┐ │ region │ countries_with_gdp │ mean_gdp │ │ varchar │ int64 │ double │ ├───────────────┼────────────────────┼──────────┤ │ North America │ 1 │ 59534.0 │ │ Europe │ 1 │ 42373.0 │ │ East Asia │ 1 │ 10573.0 │ │ Latin America │ 1 │ 8435.0 │ │ South Asia │ 1 │ 1807.0 │ │ Oceania │ 0 │ NULL │ └───────────────┴────────────────────┴──────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Appendix 02: Practice at home: GROUP BY and HAVING {#sec-appendix-02} ### One more question to try on your own :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="46%"} Which countries have had the highest life expectancy since 2010? 1. Create the `wdi` view over the panel 2. Keep only the `life_expectancy` rows 3. Keep only the years from 2010 onwards 4. Compute the mean of `value` for each country 5. Keep the countries whose mean is above 82 6. Sort from highest to lowest 7. Return the top five, rounded to one decimal ::: :::{.column width="54%"} :::{style="font-size: 20px;"} ::: {#17bdbdb2 .cell cache='true' execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, ROUND(AVG(value), 1) AS mean_life_exp FROM wdi WHERE indicator = 'life_expectancy' AND year >= 2010 GROUP BY country HAVING AVG(value) > 82 ORDER BY mean_life_exp DESC LIMIT 5 """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ``` ┌──────────────────────┬───────────────┐ │ country │ mean_life_exp │ │ varchar │ double │ ├──────────────────────┼───────────────┤ │ Monaco │ 85.5 │ │ San Marino │ 84.4 │ │ Hong Kong SAR, China │ 84.3 │ │ Japan │ 83.8 │ │ Andorra │ 83.8 │ └──────────────────────┴───────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: - `WHERE` drops rows, `HAVING AVG(value) > 82` tests the group - `ORDER BY` names `mean_life_exp`, the alias created in `SELECT` - Hong Kong and Japan are the only places in the top five with more than a million people ::: ::: :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 15px;"} [[Back to Next class]{.button}](#sec-next-class) ::: ::: ## Appendix 03: When something goes wrong {#sec-appendix-03} :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 19px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} [`Parser Error: syntax error at or near ".."`]{.alert} The file path is not quoted. Put single quotes around it: `FROM '../data/f.parquet'`. [`IO Error: No files found that match the pattern`]{.alert} The path is quoted but wrong. Paths are relative to the working directory (the notebook's folder in Jupyter), so check with `os.getcwd()`. [`Binder Error: Referenced column "gdp" not found`]{.alert} The column name is misspelled or does not exist. Run `DESCRIBE SELECT * FROM wdi` and read the list ::: :::{.column width="50%"} [`Parser Error: syntax error at or near "SELCT"`]{.alert} A keyword is misspelled. DuckDB quotes the offending word back at you, so read the message to the end. [`Binder Error` on a value you know exists]{.alert} You wrote `WHERE indicator = "gdp_per_capita"` with double quotes. Double quotes mean a column name in SQL, single quotes mean text. [`Catalog Error: Table with name wdi does not exist`]{.alert} The view lives in the session that created it. Re-run the `CREATE VIEW` cell after restarting Python ::: ::: :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 15px;"} [[Back to Next class]{.button}](#sec-next-class) ::: ::: ## Appendix 04: Grouping by two columns {#sec-appendix-04} ### Every combination that exists in the data :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - Name two columns and you get one row for each pair that appears in the filtered rows - Two countries and two indicators give four rows here - Combinations with no rows never appear. SQL does not invent empty groups - Japan's mean life expectancy since 2010 is nine years above Brazil's. Its CO2 per person is almost four times higher - A mean over years like this weights every year equally. Say so when you report it ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 22px;"} ::: {#64d2e714 .cell cache='true' execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, indicator, ROUND(AVG(value), 1) AS mean_value FROM wdi WHERE year >= 2010 AND country IN ('Brazil', 'Japan') AND indicator IN ('life_expectancy', 'co2_per_capita') GROUP BY country, indicator ORDER BY country, indicator """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ``` ┌─────────┬─────────────────┬────────────┐ │ country │ indicator │ mean_value │ │ varchar │ varchar │ double │ ├─────────┼─────────────────┼────────────┤ │ Brazil │ co2_per_capita │ 2.4 │ │ Brazil │ life_expectancy │ 74.8 │ │ Japan │ co2_per_capita │ 9.3 │ │ Japan │ life_expectancy │ 83.8 │ └─────────┴─────────────────┴────────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 15px;"} [[Back to GROUP BY]{.button}](#sec-group-by) ::: ::: ## Appendix 05: Anti-joins and UNION {#sec-appendix-05} ### Finding rows with no partner :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 19px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="44%"} - An [anti-join]{.alert} asks which rows on the left have no partner on the right - `NOT EXISTS` runs a small query for each row and keeps the row when it returns nothing - Japan is the only such row here, because `JPN` is missing from `regions` - A join adds columns. [`UNION`]{.alert} stacks rows from two results that have the same columns - `UNION` removes duplicate rows, `UNION ALL` keeps them and is faster - The tagged result has five rows: Germany, Japan and the United States rich, Brazil and India poor - China falls in neither band, so it appears in no row at all ::: :::{.column width="56%"} :::{style="font-size: 20px;"} ::: {#0e9a2694 .cell cache='true' execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT g.country, g.iso3 FROM gdp2020 AS g WHERE NOT EXISTS ( SELECT 1 FROM regions AS r WHERE r.iso3 = g.iso3 ) """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ``` ┌─────────┬─────────┐ │ country │ iso3 │ │ varchar │ varchar │ ├─────────┼─────────┤ │ Japan │ JPN │ └─────────┴─────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: {#916c4dd2 .cell cache='true' execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} duckdb.sql(""" SELECT country, 'rich' AS tag FROM gdp2020 WHERE gdp_per_capita > 30000 UNION SELECT country, 'poor' AS tag FROM gdp2020 WHERE gdp_per_capita < 10000 ORDER BY country """) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ``` ┌───────────────┬─────────┐ │ country │ tag │ │ varchar │ varchar │ ├───────────────┼─────────┤ │ Brazil │ poor │ │ Germany │ rich │ │ India │ poor │ │ Japan │ rich │ │ United States │ rich │ └───────────────┴─────────┘ ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 15px;"} [[Back to the exercise solution]{.button}](#sec-appendix-01) ::: ::: ## Appendix 06: When SQL beats a DataFrame {#sec-appendix-06} ### A checklist for each tool :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 21px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} Reach for SQL when: - You are joining two or more tables - You are filtering and aggregating a file that is larger than your RAM - The question is a `GROUP BY` with a couple of conditions - Someone else has to read the query. A colleague who has never seen pandas can still read your `SELECT` - The data already lives in a database ::: :::{.column width="50%"} Stay in pandas when: - You need row-by-row logic that has no set-based version - You are plotting, or feeding a model - You want many small inspectable steps, each one a variable you can look at - The reshaping is the hard part, as in the `pivot` in the DuckDB and pandas section :::{style="background: rgba(27, 58, 107, 0.08); padding: 12px; border-radius: 10px; font-size: 19px; margin-top: 12px;"} Want more practice? The course website has a full self-study [DuckDB SQL tutorial](https://danilofreire.github.io/datasci350/04-duckdb-sql-tutorial.html) covering everything on these slides in more depth ::: ::: ::: :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 15px;"} [[Back to the pandas slide]{.button}](#sec-pandas) ::: ::: ## Appendix 07: The benchmark query {#sec-appendix-07} ### The query and where the timings come from :::{style="margin-top: 40px; font-size: 20px;"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} - The DuckDB version is the query you already know, with a file path in `FROM` and a `GROUP BY` at the end - The data is `wdi_big.parquet`, a synthetic panel of 200,681,600 rows built by cloning the small panel many times - The file is not committed, and the script that rebuilds it is in [`data/make_big_parquet.py`](https://github.com/danilofreire/datasci350/blob/main/lectures/lecture-22/data/make_big_parquet.py) - The timings were measured once and saved to [`data/benchmark_results.csv`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/danilofreire/datasci350/main/lectures/lecture-22/data/benchmark_results.csv). The deck reads that file rather than re-running anything - pandas loads the whole thing and calls `groupby`, Dask uses a parallel DataFrame, and DuckDB runs SQL straight over the file ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 22px;"} ::: {#043bc242 .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} import duckdb duckdb.sql(""" SELECT indicator, (year // 10) * 10 AS decade, AVG(value) AS mean_value FROM 'data/wdi_big.parquet' WHERE year >= 1990 GROUP BY indicator, decade """).df() ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::{style="text-align: center; margin-top: 15px;"} [[Back to the benchmark]{.button}](#sec-benchmark) ::: :::
